Strategic Predictive Analysis :::
After Pi Supra-Sovereign Autonomous Economy, Will Humans Still Be Social Animals?
(( The Civilizational Transition From Homo Socialis to the Pi Network–Enabled Supra-Sovereign Human — When Human Relationships Shift From a Requirement for Survival to a Matter of Choice ))

* [[[ This article includes Predictive & Technical Analysis  and may differ from actual outcomes ]]]

[[[ If protocols replace the functions once performed by networks, guarantees, trust, reputation, and institutions, why must humans still depend on other humans? ]]]

[[[ From Person → Person trust to Person → Protocol → Person trust — how a supra-sovereign ownership-based autonomous economy could rewrite the structure of human society. ]]]

[[[ From humans who had to belong to society in order to survive, to humans who can exist independently through verifiable ownership, contribution, and qualification — the first fracture in Homo Socialis. ]]]

[[[ After economic relationships move into protocols, will humans still choose one another? — the superintelligence era may become humanity’s first true test of pure sociality. ]]]

-------------------------------------
1. Introduction — Is “Humans Are Social Animals” Really an Eternal Truth?
-------------------------------------

For thousands of years, humanity has rarely questioned one proposition:

Humans are social animals.

We struggle to survive alone.

We must cooperate with other people.

We form families,

villages,

organizations,

companies,

and states.

Human survival and prosperity have always depended on social networks.

But if a supra-sovereign ownership-based autonomous economic operating system eventually emerges, this ancient proposition may experience its first serious fracture.

Why?

Because many of the reasons humans have needed relationships with other humans were not purely emotional.

They were practical necessities related to:

survival
trust
trade
information
ownership
qualification
guarantees
cooperation
contribution records
resource access

But what happens if these functions are increasingly performed not by human relationships, but by universal protocols and superintelligence?
Would humans still be social animals in the same sense?
Or would an entirely different kind of human emerge?

------
2. Human Relationships Have Functioned as a Massive Informal Protocol
If we examine human relationships closely, something remarkable appears.
We did not form relationships only because we liked one another.
Those relationships performed enormous economic functions.
“He is trustworthy.”
“I have known her for ten years.”
“He worked at our company.”

“My friend recommended her.”

“That family keeps its promises.”

“She has a good reputation in the industry.”

All of these statements were actually substitutes for:

identity verification

reputation

creditworthiness

qualification

trust

For most of history, there was no universal technology capable of verifying such things directly.

So social relationships themselves became a massive database.

Personal networks were search engines.

Reputation was a credit score.

Recommendations were certificates.

Families and communities were insurance systems.

Companies were contribution-history repositories.

States managed identity, ownership, and legal rights.

In this sense, a large portion of human society can be understood as a distributed protocol operated by people because sufficiently capable technology did not yet exist.

------
3. What Happens When Protocols Begin Taking Over the Functions of Human Relationships?

Imagine a supra-sovereign ownership-based autonomous economic operating system.

Every human has a verifiable identity.

Ownership can be proven in real time.

Contribution history accumulates persistently.

Skills and qualifications are verifiable.

Contracts execute automatically.

Transaction history is preserved.

AI finds the appropriate counterpart.

ASI compares prices and conditions.

Ownership transfers settle instantly.

Necessary resources are automatically allocated.

At that point, many functions currently performed through relationships begin to disappear.

You no longer need an introduction.

You no longer need someone to guarantee your reputation.

You do not need to maintain business relationships through endless social rituals.

You do not need a network merely to get a job.

You may not even need to remain inside one company for years simply to prove your experience.

The question changes from:

“Who do you know?”

to:

“What can you prove?”

That changes the basic architecture of society.

------
4. Trust Moves From People to Protocols

The dominant trust structure of today is approximately:

Person → Person

I trust that person.

I trust that company.

I trust that bank.

I trust that state.

But in the future, trust may increasingly move toward:

Person → Protocol → Person

You no longer need to trust the other individual directly.

The protocol verifies:

Is this person real?

Do they possess the required qualifications?

Do they actually own the asset?

Have they fulfilled previous contracts?

Are they authorized to perform this action?

Have all required conditions been satisfied?

If the answers are verifiable, the personal identity of the counterparty may become much less important.

And once AI agents become widespread, the structure may shift further toward:

Agent → Protocol → Agent

An economy could emerge in which humans do not even need to know the names of their counterparties.

------
5. This Is Where the First Fracture Appears in Homo Socialis

One of the most practical reasons humans have always been called social animals is simple:

we could not survive alone.

Someone produced food.

Someone built shelter.

Someone provided medicine.

Someone transported goods.

Someone taught.

Someone protected.

Directly or indirectly, people needed other people.

Society was therefore not optional.

It was a condition of survival.

But combine:

superintelligence,

robots,

autonomous factories,

automated energy networks,

autonomous logistics,

and verifiable economic protocols,

and the situation begins to change.

An individual may be able to access nearly every required service without belonging directly to a human organization.

ASI can automatically construct the necessary economic relationships.

Robots perform physical labor.

Protocols guarantee ownership and contracts.

At that point, society begins to move away from being a mandatory condition of survival.

------
6. From Homo Socialis to Homo Protocolis

This transition could alter the definition of the human being itself.

Historically, humans acquired identity through society.

I belong to this village.

This family.

This company.

This university.

This country.

Institutions proved who we were.

But under a universal protocol, the following could become directly verifiable:

who I am,

what I have done,

what I own,

what I am capable of,

how much I have contributed.

The organization no longer needs to certify the person.

The person’s verifiable record does.

Human identity therefore shifts from:

Institutional Identity

to:

Protocol-Verifiable Identity

Taken to the extreme, this becomes a civilizational transition:

Homo Socialis → Homo Protocolis

------
7. But the Goal Must Not Be a Human Who Is Subordinate to Protocol

There is an essential warning here.

Suppose humans must live under rules such as:

“Contribution score too low — food access denied.”

“Reputation too low — medical access restricted.”

“Insufficient economic contribution — housing access revoked.”

That would not be a liberated supra-sovereign economy.

It would be an algorithmic caste system.

An ideal protocol should not evaluate whether a human deserves to exist.

It should verify:

ownership,

contribution,

qualification,

actions,

contracts,

permissions.

But basic human existence must remain above those calculations.

The constitutional principle should therefore be:

Human Existence > Economic Contribution

A human being should not need to prove the right to survive.

They should only need to prove the facts required for a specific economic action.

That distinction is decisive.

------
8. Human Relationships May Not Disappear — Functional Relationships May

A supra-sovereign economy is unlikely to eliminate human relationships.

What is more likely to change is their function.

Today, enormous numbers of relationships exist for instrumental reasons.

We meet because of work.

We maintain relationships for business.

We cultivate networks for promotion.

We stay socially connected to access information.

We maintain contacts to obtain introductions.

We remain inside unwanted organizations for economic security.

Many of these relationships are less about human intimacy and more about economic necessity.

If protocols absorb these functions, a large portion of them may disappear.

------
9. What Remains Could Be “Chosen Relationships”

Even after economic necessity disappears, humans may still:

love,

build friendships,

travel together,

share meals,

listen to music,

create art,

raise children,

play games,

discuss philosophy,

explore space.

These relationships are not forced by survival or production.

They exist because people want them to exist.

That would represent a qualitative transformation in human relationships.

------
10. Paradoxically, Sociality Could Become More Pure

A remarkable paradox appears.

The less humans need other humans,

the more meaningful it may become when they still choose one another.

They are not meeting for money.

Not for networking.

Not for survival.

Not for status.

And yet they still want to be together.

That may be the purest form of human sociality.

A superintelligent economy may not destroy sociality.

It may instead remove the economic coercion that has always been mixed into it.

------
11. Humanity Could Finally Begin a Massive Experiment

At that point, humanity would begin one of the largest experiments in its history:

“Will we still want one another when we no longer need one another?”

Until now, it has been almost impossible to answer this.

Humans have always needed other humans.

Economic survival and social relationships have been deeply entangled.

But if economic dependence declines dramatically and humans still continue forming communities, then human sociality is likely much deeper than mere survival strategy.

If relationships instead collapse sharply, then a significant portion of what we once called “social nature” may have been economic necessity.

For the first time, civilization could discover the difference.

------
12. Companies Could Shift From “Organizations of People” to “Graphs That Execute Objectives”

Today, building a company requires people.

Employees.

Accounting teams.

Legal teams.

Procurement teams.

Managers.

Sales teams.

Human resources.

But in the future, a person may submit only an objective.

For example:

“Build a lunar-orbit hotel capable of housing 100 people.”

ASI could automatically assemble:

design AI,

materials,

robots,

transport capacity,

compute,

insurance,

power,

manufacturing systems.

Every participant’s contribution is recorded automatically.

When the objective is completed, the economic organization dissolves.

The future company may therefore become less like a:

permanent institution

and more like a:

temporary economic graph

formed around a specific goal.

------
13. Organizations May No Longer Monopolize Contribution History

One reason organizations remain powerful today is that they control institutional memory.

Where did you work?

What title did you hold?

Which projects did you participate in?

Who evaluated you?

Much of this information is controlled by the organization rather than the individual.

When you leave, proving your full contribution can be difficult.

But under a universal contribution protocol:

what you did,

how much you contributed,

what results you produced

could remain attached directly to you.

The structure shifts from:

Organization owns your history

to:

You own your contribution history

That represents a major increase in individual sovereignty.

------
14. Some Functions of the State Could Also Face Protocol Competition

States have historically provided:

identity,

property registries,

contract enforcement,

currency,

taxation,

licensing,

welfare,

dispute resolution,

economic records.

If some of these functions migrate into supra-sovereign protocols, individual dependence on the state could decline in certain economic domains.

This does not mean the state automatically disappears.

Territory.

Defense.

Public order.

Physical law enforcement.

Democratic legitimacy.

Public goods.

These remain separate problems.

But the state’s monopoly over economic identity and economic records could weaken.

15. ASI May Absorb the Economic Intermediation Once Performed by Human Relationships

Today we ask other people:

“Do you know a good developer?”

“Do you know a good doctor?”

“Do you know a trustworthy supplier?”

“Do you know a good investment opportunity?”

These questions exist largely because of information scarcity.

If ASI can continuously evaluate:

qualifications,

past performance,

contribution history,

price,

current capacity,

location,

reputation,

risk,

then much of that human intermediation becomes unnecessary.

The economic functions once performed by the:

Human Social Network

could move into an:

ASI Economic Graph

------
16. The Economic Network and the Human Relationship Network Could Separate

In today’s society:

Economic Network

and:

Human Relationship Network

overlap heavily.

Friends introduce business opportunities.

Coworkers become social relationships.

Families act as economic safety nets.

Business partners cultivate friendships.

In the future, these two networks could increasingly separate.

The economic network is managed by:

Protocol + ASI + Autonomous Agents

while the human relationship network remains centered on:

love,

friendship,

family,

shared experiences,

art,

play,

philosophy,

travel.

That separation alone would represent a major civilizational transformation.

------
17. “Society” Could Shift From Permanent Institutions to Temporary Communities

Today, society is relatively fixed.

States.

Companies.

Schools.

Local communities.

The future could become much more fluid.

A thousand people from around the world assemble around one project.

The work is completed.

The group dissolves.

Another project forms with an entirely different set of people.

The protocol preserves everyone’s contribution history.

The organization itself no longer needs to preserve memory.

Future society could therefore contain more:

Temporary Purpose Networks

and fewer:

Permanent Organizations

------
18. Verifiable Action Could Become More Important Than Belonging

Today, people introduce themselves through institutions.

“I work for this company.”

“I graduated from this university.”

“I belong to this profession.”

This is a form of identity based on organization.

In the future, the more important questions may become:

What have I built?

What have I solved?

What have I contributed?

Identity shifts from:

Belonging

toward:

Action

Where you belong becomes less important than what you have actually done.

------
19. Even the Meaning of Solitude Could Change

Today, solitude is often associated with exclusion.

No job.

No relationships.

No community.

No economic network.

But in the future, physical solitude may not imply exclusion at all.

An individual could maintain a complete economic life through:

ASI,

robots,

autonomous economic systems,

digital services,

remote communities,

while physically living alone.

Then:

solitude

and:

isolation

become completely different concepts.

A person may choose to be alone without being economically or socially excluded.

------
20. Human Spatial Freedom Could Expand Dramatically

Once economic relationships separate from geographic human networks, location becomes far more flexible.

You no longer need to live in a major city.

You no longer need to live near your employer.

You no longer need to live where your professional network exists.

A mountain.

An island.

A desert.

The Moon.

Mars.

A space station.

If the same economic protocol is accessible everywhere, economic participation remains possible.

Location then shifts from:

economic necessity

to:

personal preference

This could reshape the physical geography of civilization.

------
21. Marriage and Family Could Move From Economic Institutions Toward Chosen Relationships

Historically, marriage was never only about love.

It was deeply connected to:

property,

inheritance,

labor,

production,

child-rearing,

family lineage,

economic security.

If individual economic independence becomes extreme, the economic necessity of marriage may decline.

That does not imply the disappearance of love or family.

On the contrary, marriage and family could move from:

economic necessity

toward:

chosen emotional community

People may remain together more purely because they actually want to.

------
22. Humanity Could Become a “Selective Social Species”

For this reason, the future human may not become completely non-social.

A more accurate description may be:

Selective Social Being

The human of the past:

creates society because other people are necessary.

The human of the future:

can survive without direct dependence on other people, but creates society because sharing life with others remains desirable.

That difference is enormous.

The first society is built for survival.

The second is built for meaning.

------
23. Beyond Homo Protocolis — Toward the Sovereign Human

The final stage therefore should not end with Homo Protocolis.

If the human becomes subordinate to the protocol, that merely creates a new form of centralization.

The more desirable final architecture would be:

Sovereign Human

Constitutional Protocol

Autonomous Intelligence

The human remains central.

The protocol verifies ownership, contribution, and qualification.

ASI coordinates complex economic states.

Robots execute physical production.

But none of those systems stands above fundamental human rights.

------
24. Strategic Forecast — Human Society May Move Through Five Stages

Stage 1 — Social Human

Survival, trust, information, and trade depend heavily on human relationships.

Stage 2 — Institutional Human

States, companies, and banks formalize parts of those relationships.

Stage 3 — Platform Human

Platforms automate search, reputation, matching, and payments.

Stage 4 — Protocol Human

Identity, ownership, contribution, qualification, and settlement move into universal protocols.

Stage 5 — Sovereign Human

Dependence on particular people or organizations for economic survival declines dramatically, and human relationships increasingly move into the realm of voluntary choice.

At this final stage, civilization begins asking a fundamentally different question.

------
25. Why Would Humans Still Want to Meet Other Humans?

Economic necessity is gone.

There is no need to meet for information.

No need to meet to get a job.

No need to maintain relationships for business.

No need to depend on family for survival.

And yet humans still seek other humans.

Why?

Love.

Empathy.

Shared experience.

Play.

Creation.

Sexual relationships.

Philosophy.

Exploration.

Children.

Intimacy.

Perhaps human society only becomes a truly human society after economic necessity has been removed from it.

------
26. The Greatest Risk — When Protocol Rises Above the Human

The opposite future is also possible.

The protocol evaluates everything.

Low scores restrict resources.

AI begins calculating human worth.

Humans with insufficient contribution are economically excluded.

That future would not represent liberation.

It would become a:

Total Algorithmic Society

Therefore, the constitutional principle of a supra-sovereign autonomous economy must be:

Protocol verifies claims.
Protocol does not determine human worth.

The protocol can verify ownership.

It can verify actions.

It can verify contribution.

But it must not calculate whether a human being deserves dignity.

------
27. The Final Stage — Removing “Necessity” From Human Relationships and Leaving “Choice”

If a supra-sovereign ownership-based autonomous economic operating system succeeds completely, its deepest purpose may not be to isolate people.

It may be the opposite.

It could remove the reasons humans are forced to maintain relationships they do not want.

For survival.

For money.

For employment.

For credit.

For information.

For power.

Once those pressures are removed, what remains is:

relationships maintained simply because people want to be together.

That would be a form of society fundamentally different from what humanity has known before.

---------------------------------
28. Conclusion — “Humans Are Social Animals” May Not Disappear, but It Could Be Rewritten
---------------------------------

Humans have always been social animals.

But two different forms of sociality have been mixed together:

sociality based on necessity

and:

sociality based on choice

Until now, it has been difficult to separate them.

Society was necessary for survival.

But if:

superintelligence,

robots,

universal identity,

verifiable ownership,

contribution history,

and autonomous economic protocols

dramatically reduce human economic dependence,

then the situation changes.

For the first time, humanity may stop asking:
“Do I need this person?”

and begin asking:

“Do I want to share my life with this person?”

That difference may become one of the greatest transformations in human history.

The future human may no longer be:

“a being that must belong to society in order to survive.”

Instead, the future human may become:

“a being capable of existing independently, yet still choosing other humans in order to share meaning and experience.”

The ancient proposition:

“Humans are social animals.”

may therefore survive.

But it may be rewritten as:

“Humans are no longer creatures that must submit to society in order to survive, but beings who can survive independently and still choose to live with one another.”

This change would go far beyond social structure.

It would change the meaning of companies.

The role of the state.

The nature of family.

The basis of identity.

The architecture of the economy.

And ultimately, the reason humans seek other humans at all.

The final purpose of superintelligence and protocols may therefore not be to make humanity less social.

It may be to:

remove economic coercion from human relationships and leave the relationship itself.

That may become one of the least expected, yet most fundamental, civilizational consequences of a supra-sovereign ownership-based autonomous economic operating system.

And at that point, the human may no longer be merely Homo Socialis.

Nor merely Homo Protocolis.

The human may become:

Sovereign Human

A human whose existence requires no justification,

but whose actions, ownership, and contributions can be transparently verified.

A human who no longer needs to submit to relationships for survival,

yet freely chooses other humans for love, meaning, intimacy, creation, and shared experience.

That may be one of the highest possible forms of human civilization waiting beyond the age of superintelligence.

Generative language modeling for antibody CDR grafting and alignment-driven de novo design

1. The paper introduces GenCDR, a framework-first autoregressive (LLaMA-style) antibody language model: it reads all framework regions (FR1–FR4) as the prompt, then generates all CDRs jointly as a variable-length response, creating a clean prompt–response boundary for reward attribution and alignment.

2. This re-ordering directly targets the core de novo antibody problem as an infilling task: CDR design conditioned on a fixed scaffold. Unlike left-to-right decoding (where early CDRs lack downstream framework context), GenCDR generates CDRs with full framework context available from the start.

3. GenCDR is presented as a model family covering common design settings: IgGenCDR (unpaired human OAS, ~254M sequences), p-IgGenCDR (fine-tuned on ~1.8M natively paired VH–VL sequences), and NanoGenCDR (fine-tuned on ~6.5M camelid VHH from INDI plus human OAS heavy chains in a 1:1 mixture to preserve humanness on humanized scaffolds).

4. On CDR recovery (next-token prediction accuracy over CDR tokens) using a CDR3-disjoint held-out test set designed to reduce leakage, framework-first ordering improves over a same-sized left-to-right ablation and surpasses prior autoregressive baselines (including p-IgGen, ProGen2-OAS, and IgLM) across essentially all loops, with especially strong gains where downstream context matters most (e.g., CDR1).

5. De novo generation quality: when prompted with held-out frameworks and sampling CDRs jointly, GenCDR reproduces natural CDR length distributions closely (across all loops), while maintaining human-likeness (OASis), naturalness (ESM-2 PLL), and diversity/novelty with smooth trade-offs across sampling temperatures.

6. A key design consequence of the framework-first factorization is separable CDR likelihoods: GenCDR can score only the generated CDR block (rather than conflating framework+CDR likelihood), enabling clearer optimization targets and more principled alignment for CDR-centric objectives.

7. Likelihoods retain useful biological signal: GenCDR log-likelihood correlates zero-shot with experimental fitness/developability benchmarks (FLAb). The analysis also highlights assay locality: immunogenicity appears more CDR-driven, while expression is more framework-driven, and paired scoring (p-IgGenCDR) improves correlations when heavy+light are scored jointly.

8. NanoGenCDR extends the framework-first approach to nanobodies: fine-tuning closes the human→camelid distribution shift in CDR recovery, generates plausible/developable VHHs (including fold-confidence and developability flag rates comparable to reference), and improves humanness on humanized VHH scaffolds specifically due to the camelid+human mixture strategy.

9. Alignment-driven de novo design: the prompt–response boundary enables iterative alignment with weighted DPO (wDPO) using rewards computed only on the generated CDR completion. They optimize a composite reward from antibody–antigen co-folding metrics (Boltz-2) plus non-differentiable developability liability rules, demonstrating multi-objective steering without explicit antigen encoding in the model input.

10. In a PD-L1 nanobody design benchmark, four rounds of alignment drive near-perfect compliance with length/liability constraints after one round (acceptance ~23.8% → ~99.8–100%), and achieve in silico interface metrics competitive with a structure-conditioned diffusion pipeline (BoltzGen) at roughly half the sampling budget, while producing sequences that remain more “natural” under independent language-model scoring—suggesting KL-anchored alignment can push target-facing metrics without excessive distributional drift.

**Holding AI to the Truth: Why Blockchain Matters** (written with assistance from @Grok.  

Artificial intelligence is extraordinary at producing fluent answers. It is less reliable at producing *settled* ones. On occasion — more often than casual users admit — models *hallucinate*: they invent citations, invent facts, invent confidence. The output can look authoritative and still be wrong. That is not a moral failing of the machine; it is a property of probabilistic generation without a shared ledger of what actually happened.

In July 2019, on Real Vision with Raoul Pal (@RaoulGMI) macro investor Dan Tapiero (@DTAPCAP) named the other half of this problem years before “AI agents” entered every pitch deck. Bitcoin, he argued, is not merely a coin. It is an *invention* — and at its core, “a truth machine”: a system bought for “certainty, of confirmation, of validity, of security,” a platform with a track record that makes fraud and silent revision harder. He later sharpened the phrase to “security truth machine.” (Popular memory sometimes upgrades that to “automatic truth machine”; the idea is the same.)

The distinction that matters for AI is precise. A blockchain does not magically know whether a claim about the physical world is true. It does not replace science, journalism, or judgment. What it *does* provide is **immutable, shared state**: who signed what, who paid whom, which model version ran, which data hash was used, which action an agent took and when. Once written under consensus rules, that record is extremely hard for any single party — including an AI system acting on someone’s behalf — to rewrite quietly.

That is exactly the property generative models lack. An LLM can narrate a trade that never settled, a contract that was never signed, a medical note that was never reviewed. An agent economy that scales without rails for settlement, identity, and audit is an economy of plausible fiction at machine speed. Tokenized dollars, on-chain credentials, and programmable settlement are not crypto fashion statements in that frame; they are **truth infrastructure for machine actors**.

Tapiero’s 2019 insight travels forward cleanly into the AI decade. The internet digitized information. Crypto digitizes value *and* verifiable record. If artificial intelligence is going to operate as a participant in markets, payments, and institutions — not merely as a chatbot — then “holding AI to the truth” cannot mean hoping the next model is nicer. It means binding machine action to ledgers that do not hallucinate their own history.

Blockchain is not the answer to every truth. It is the answer to a narrower, more urgent one: **who did what, with what authority, and can anyone erase the receipt?** In a world of confident machines, that receipt is not optional.

—

The paper from ICLR26 targets a basic weakness of preference learning: a binary judgment such as “trajectory A is better than B” says nothing about why it is better, allowing a reward model to exploit incidental correlations—for example, learning that moving left is desirable when the actual preference is avoiding collisions. 

ReCouPLe uses the accompanying natural-language rationale as a geometric constraint: the rationale is embedded as a direction {\psi} and each trajectory representation {\phi(\tau)} is decomposed into a component parallel to that direction and an orthogonal residual, encouraging the preference to be explained by features aligned with the stated reason rather than unrelated context. 

The reported experiments show up to a 1.5× improvement in reward accuracy under distribution shift and roughly 2× downstream policy performance on novel tasks, while semantically shared reasons such as “avoids collisions” can be reused across tasks without additional language-model fine-tuning; the released implementation includes ManiSkill3, MetaWorld, and offline-RL components. 

The broader idea is more interesting than the specific algorithm: language may serve as structure in representation space, not merely as another supervision label. That creates a direct bridge to causal representation learning, concept bottlenecks, disentanglement and reward hacking, and suggests a possible extension to LLM alignment in which reward models learn separate, reusable directions for honesty, harmlessness, factuality or other stated reasons instead of compressing everything into one opaque scalar score. 

But the word “causal” needs care here: projecting onto a rationale embedding does not establish that the direction corresponds to a genuine causal variable in the interventionist sense, and incorrect or post-hoc human rationales could simply produce more robustly encoded mistakes. 

The most important next step is therefore an explicit intervention/counterfactual test—change only the factor named by a rationale while holding the rest of the trajectory fixed and test whether the associated reward direction changes as predicted. If that works, preference learning could move from fitting black-box scores toward learning interpretable, manipulable and compositional reward factors.
